chat.author: Mark Andrews
chat.text: Hundreds of millions of home users have gone from IPv4 only to dual stack without knowing they have gone to dual stack.  Basically it was just turned on by the ISP and CPE announced IPv6 was available.  The world didn't fall over.

chat.author: Daniel Bernier
chat.text: Managers care about ROI of a technology shift either in OPEX savings or Revenu increase.

chat.author: Mark Andrews
chat.text: The boxes they have are dual stack capable to day.

chat.author: Daniel Bernier
chat.text: Infrastructure people want to transition because it eases the IPv4 maintenance, overlap challenges with common services and scarcity of available addresses.

chat.author: Mark Andrews
chat.text: Going IPv6 only is harder because you have to ensure all your equipment supports it.

chat.author: Antonios Chariton
chat.text: IPv6 and WiFi Multicast has always been a bit challenging. In RADIUS assigned VLANs for many WiFi deployments by default devices will get addresses via SLAAC from all VLANs with at least one wireless device in them. They won’t work, and Apple devices will ignore them, but it breaks Android. If these were converted, too, it would also be fine.

chat.author: Ondřej Caletka
chat.text: Oh yeah, leaking broadcasts/multicasts between VLANs on some APs has been a problem for years already. Which is a bit sad.

chat.author: Nick Buraglio
chat.text: I have also seen this across certain merchant silicon managed switches. It's quite horrible

chat.author: Nick Buraglio
chat.text: Specifically, a few L2 managed switches that are popular in hospitality and WISP networks

chat.author: Kyle Rose
chat.text: That is pretty awful. Having to be bug-for-bug compatible with the long tail of broken hardware is not a good way to run a railroad, and yet... here we are.
